newsitem.title: SWITZERLAND: Cyberspace copyright talks hit fresh snags.
newsitem.headline: Cyberspace copyright talks hit fresh snags.

text.p: After nearly three weeks, global talks to rewrite copyright rules for cyberspace were bogged down on Thursday, raising doubts that the contentious treaties can be passed by a Friday deadline, negotiators said.

Voting on the treaties was supposed to begin on Thursday, but talks were delayed to allow time to solve disputes between copyright-based industries, such as music, and online companies over exemptions from rules in the digital era.

"It's quite intense. After three weeks of talks, the real meat of the negotiations has really started," said Adrian Strain of the music industry lobby group, the International Federation of the Phonographic Industry (IFPI).
IFPI's 1,100 members include big record producers BMG, EMI, MCA, Sony Music and PolyGram.

Under the auspices of the U.N.s' World Intellectual Property Organisation which coordinates copyrights, the talks cover three treaties -- on literary and artistic works, on rights of performers and producers of music, and database producers.

They aim to upgrade the century-old Berne convention on copyrights to cover the borderless world of Internet, which has ripped up rulebooks as it can copy and distribute anything from music to software at the click of a computer mouse.

Music, entertainment and software industries, trying to ensure they profit from works distributed electronically, are enthusiastic supporters of the treaties which they say provide a legal basis for commercial use of their products on the Internet.
But online and Internet giants are furious that the treaties make even innocent Web-surfing, which by definition requires that a computer make transient copies, a copyright violation.
Copyright officials say that online companies have nothing to fear from the treaties, but the Internet industry wants the treaties to spell out their legal protection.

Internet and online service providers say the pacts expose them to multi-billion-dollar liability for copyright violations by millions of service users and give sweeping powers to copyright-based industries like music and entertainment.
They want the most contentious parts deleted altogether.
Telecommunications giants such as Bell Atlantic, America Online and Nymex say they cannot police treaties that apply copyright rules to both permanent and temporary reproductions.
The $40-billion-a-year music industry raised the heat in the battle last week, accusing online companies of scaremongering to protect their multi-billion-dollar interests.

Online companies for their part allege that music and record companies want to use the Internet as a cash cow, leaving what they say is the impossible task of policing copyright violations under the proposed treaties to the Internet community.
The third treaty on databases is full of confusion and opposed by many sides and is considered dead for the time being, negotiators said.
